characters: Fosuaa: a nine-year-old Ghanaian girl with proportionate/skeletal dwarfism (shorter stature than her classmates, depicted with warmth, dignity, and natural proportions), neat braided hair with yellow beads, wearing a crisp yellow-and-blue Ghanaian primary school uniform.
Madam Esi: the kind Class Three teacher in a sky-blue and gold African-print dress.
Nuamah: a nine-year-old Ghanaian boy in a matching yellow-and-blue school uniform who stands up for Fosuaa.
Kofi (the boy who teased): a classmate in the same school uniform who apologises sincerely.

narrationPlan.voice: A gentle narrator; a clear, dignified voice for Fosuaa; a calm, warm voice for Madam Esi; a brave voice for Nuamah
narrationPlan.pace: Gentle and earnest, brightening joyfully at the end (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A soft, hopeful tune that lifts into a lively skipping rhythm at the end (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Children and adults with dwarfism are sometimes unfairly teased with names from folklore. This story states plainly that dwarfism is a natural medical condition and every classmate is a person deserving respect.
Calling people by their own name—as Fosuaa asks—models everyday dignity and inclusion.
The story honours elders’ oral traditions while drawing a firm line against using folklore to tease anyone.

Invite a disability inclusion educator or advocate to review the wording and illustrations for dignity and accuracy.

teacherGuide.overview: An inclusive school story about empathy, upstander courage, sincere apology, and why folklore must never be used to tease classmates with dwarfism or any physical difference.
learningGoals: Explain why teasing hurts and why names matter.
Demonstrate one respectful way to stand up for a classmate.
Distinguish medical facts about human diversity from folklore.
beforeReading: Ask: what makes someone feel welcome on their very first day in a new class?
whileReading: Pause after page 3: why was Nuamah brave even though he had laughed at first?
afterReading: Practise kind upstander sentences in pairs (“Stop, please use their name”).
Make a class welcome banner celebrating everyone’s strengths.
discussion: Why did Fosuaa ask her classmates to call her by her name?
What makes an apology feel genuine?
reflection: How can you help a new classmate feel included at break time?

support: Match feeling cards to how Fosuaa feels at the start, middle, and end of the story.
stretch: Write a short diary entry by Nuamah about what he learned that day.
